title: Flight Deal Tactics That Still Work — and the Ones That Never Did
metaDescription: Positioning flights, hidden-city ticketing, fare alerts, mistake fares and award routing — which flight hacks are worth the effort and which are myths.
excerpt: Some flight tricks save hundreds. Others are folklore, and a couple can get your ticket cancelled. Here is the honest sorting.
author: Trypinn Team
content:
Search for flight hacks and you get a mix of genuinely useful technique, outdated folklore from the era of published fares, and a couple of tactics that can get you banned from an airline's loyalty programme.

Here is the sorting, with the honest risk attached to each.

## Works: Fare Alerts, Set Early and Broadly

The highest-return, lowest-effort tactic in travel. Set alerts as soon as a trip is a vague idea, on multiple date combinations and multiple airports. Then stop searching.

Manual searching produces two bad outcomes: you see a price, hesitate, watch it rise, and buy in panic — or you check daily for a month and develop an emotional relationship with a number. Alerts invert this. Months of price movement arrive in your inbox, and you act on a signal instead of a mood.

## Works: Flexible Date and Map Search

A month-view calendar or a map search showing where you can fly for a given budget will consistently show a wider spread than you expect — €200 differences across adjacent days on the same route are routine, driven by which fare buckets remain.

If your dates have any give at all, search the month, not the day.

## Works: Positioning Flights

Flying a cheap short leg to start your international journey from a different airport. A long-haul fare from a major hub can be hundreds less than from your regional airport, easily covering the cost of getting there.

The catch is that a positioning flight on a **separate ticket** carries no protection. If it is delayed, the airline operating the long-haul owes you nothing. The rule: position the night before, stay near the airport, and treat the saving as paying for a hotel night. Positioning on the same day is how people miss expensive flights.

![Flights travel](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1570630358718-4fb324824b3d?fm=webp&w=1200&q=60)

## Works, With Real Risk: Hidden-City Ticketing

Booking a flight with a connection and getting off at the connecting city, because that itinerary is cheaper than flying there directly. It exploits the fact that hub-to-hub fares reflect competition, not distance.

It works, and it violates most airlines' conditions of carriage. The consequences, escalating in likelihood:

- **Your return leg is cancelled.** Airlines void the remainder of an itinerary once you skip a segment. This means it only ever works on a one-way.
- **You cannot check a bag**, because it goes to the final destination.
- **Frequent flyer miles can be clawed back** and accounts closed. This has been enforced.
- **Airlines have pursued travellers and agencies** who do it repeatedly.

Verdict: occasionally used once, on a one-way, hand luggage only, with a loyalty account you do not care about. Not a strategy.

## Does Not Work: The Tuesday Booking Myth

There is no consistently cheapest day to book. Large fare studies find differences well inside ordinary price noise. What does matter is the **day you fly** — midweek departures genuinely price lower than Friday and Sunday.

## Mostly Myth: Incognito Mode and VPNs

Clearing cookies does not reset a price. Airline pricing is driven by remaining inventory in each fare class, not by a cookie.

What is real is **point-of-sale pricing**: airlines price the same flight differently by market. Booking from a different country's site can genuinely be cheaper. It is also where you run into currency, card and billing-address mismatches, and some airlines cancel bookings they consider to have circumvented market pricing. Modest upside, non-trivial risk.

Use a private window because it costs nothing. Do not build a plan on it.

![Flights travel](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1616394585067-d3e824140aa1?fm=webp&w=1200&q=60)

## Works: Booking One-Ways Separately

The assumption that a return is always cheaper is a habit from an older fare system. On short-haul and with low-cost carriers, two one-ways — often on different airlines — frequently beat a return. Always price both.

On long-haul the return is usually still better, but check rather than assume.

## Works: Checking Nearby Airports Honestly

Real savings exist at secondary airports. The discipline is subtracting the true cost: transfer fare, transfer time, and whether the last train runs when you land. A saving of €50 that costs €35 and three hours is not a saving; it is a worse trip you paid slightly less for.

## Works: Award Routing, for the Patient

Alliance partners let you book one airline's seats with another's miles, and the charts do not always agree. Certain routes are dramatically cheaper through a partner programme.

This is genuinely lucrative and genuinely fiddly — it requires knowing which programmes partner with which, finding award availability, and transferring points before the seat disappears. Worth learning if you fly long-haul regularly. Not worth it for one trip a year.

## Situational: Mistake Fares

They still happen. If you chase them: book immediately, book direct with the airline where possible, and do not book non-refundable hotels for several days in case it is voided. Never contact the airline to confirm the fare is correct.

A windfall, not a plan.

## Does Not Work: Waiting for Last-Minute Flight Deals

Last-minute discounting persists in packages and cruises, where unsold inventory is worthless. It has largely gone from scheduled flights, because late bookers are price-insensitive and airlines know it.

## Works: Budget Carriers, Costed Properly

Low-cost carriers are genuinely cheap if you travel their way — one small bag, no seat selection, no changes, and an airport you can actually reach. They become expensive the moment you need a checked bag, a specific seat or a date change.

Price the whole thing, including bags and transfers, before comparing to a full-service fare. Sometimes the more expensive ticket is cheaper.

## The Meta-Tactic That Beats All of Them

**Be flexible about where you go.**

Every tactic above optimises the price of a fixed trip. The largest savings come from inverting the question: instead of "how cheaply can I get to Lisbon in June", ask "where can I go in June for under €300". Map-based and flexible-destination searches answer that, and the answer is often somewhere you would not have considered and will like just as much.

For groups this is even more powerful, because the constraint that drives cost is usually the combination of a fixed destination and fixed dates. Loosening either one collapses the price. Putting three candidate destinations and two candidate weeks side by side in a shared plan — **Trypinn** handles this well — and letting everyone react is faster than arguing toward a single option and then discovering it is expensive.
